lessons.title: Common Diseases and Parasites in Crocodiles
lessons.body: Crocodiles are tough, but in captivity they get stressed and sick. The most common killers on African farms are bacterial infections from dirty water. Watch for red belly, cloudy eyes, or white patches on the skin. These are signs of Aeromonas or Pseudomonas bacteria. If you see a crocodile floating sideways or not eating for two days, isolate it immediately. Use a 10% salt bath for 30 minutes daily for three days. For internal parasites like tapeworms, you'll see white segments in feces or a bloated belly. Dose with praziquantel at 5 mg per kg of body weight, mixed into a fish. Repeat after 14 days. External parasites like leeches are common in pond systems. Remove them by hand with tweezers, then apply gentian violet to the wound. Ticks can carry heartwater, so spray pens with acaricide every two weeks. Fungal infections look like cotton wool on the skin. Treat with potassium permanganate at 2 mg per liter as a dip for 10 minutes. Prevention is cheaper than cure: change 20% of pond water daily, keep stocking density below one crocodile per 2 square meters, and never feed spoiled meat. In Africa, many farms lose 30% of hatchlings to stress-related infections. Keep records of every death and note symptoms. That data tells you which disease is your biggest problem. Share it with your vet. A simple notebook and a pen are your first diagnostic tools.

lessons.title: Preventive Health Programs and Vaccination
lessons.body: There is no vaccine for crocodiles in most of Africa, so prevention is your only shield. Start with a strict biosecurity plan. Limit visitors. Use footbaths with 2% sodium hypochlorite at every pen entrance. Quarantine all new stock for 30 days in a separate area. During quarantine, treat with oxytetracycline at 20 mg per kg in feed for 5 days to prevent shipping fever. Test water weekly for ammonia, nitrite, and pH. Ammonia must stay below 0.5 mg per liter. If it rises, change 50% of water immediately. Vaccination is not common, but you can autogenous vaccinate against local bacteria. Your vet can culture a sick crocodile, kill the bacteria, and make a farm-specific vaccine. This costs about $200 but protects thousands. For parasites, deworm every 3 months with fenbendazole at 10 mg per kg. Keep a health calendar on the wall. Mark deworming dates, water test days, and quarantine ends. Train workers to spot early signs: a crocodile that refuses food for one day is a warning. Isolate it. Check teeth for broken jaws from fighting. Separate males during breeding season. Provide clean nesting material. In Africa, heat stress is a major killer. Build shade over 30% of each pen. Add a fan or misting system if temperatures exceed 35Â°C. Record everything. A simple notebook with dates and treatments will show you patterns. If you see three deaths in a week, call your vet immediately. Do not wait.

lessons.title: Diagnosing and Treating Infections
lessons.body: When a crocodile gets sick, you need to act fast. First, catch it safely. Use a noose pole or a net. For a 2-meter crocodile, two people are needed. Wear thick gloves. Once restrained, check its mouth, eyes, and vent. A healthy crocodile has clear eyes and pink gums. Pale gums mean anemia, often from parasites. Yellow gums mean liver damage. Take a swab from any wound or from the cloaca. Put it in a sterile tube and send it to a vet lab. In many African countries, you can use a local human hospital lab for basic culture. While waiting for results, start broad-spectrum antibiotics. Oxytetracycline at 20 mg per kg by injection into the tail muscle, every 3 days for 3 doses. For wounds, clean with dilute iodine (1 part iodine to 10 parts water) and apply honey. Honey is a natural antibiotic and works well in Africa. If the crocodile is not eating, force-feed a slurry of fish, water, and vitamins using a stomach tube. Give 10 ml per kg of body weight. For fungal infections, use a 0.5% copper sulfate dip for 5 minutes daily. For internal parasites, use praziquantel 5 mg per kg. If you suspect viral disease like poxvirus, there is no cure. Isolate and cull to save the rest. Always finish the full course of antibiotics, even if the animal looks better. Stopping early creates resistant bacteria. Keep a treatment log: date, drug, dose, and outcome. After treatment, disinfect the pen with 2% formalin. Let it dry for 24 hours before returning the crocodile. If you cannot diagnose, call your vet. A phone call is cheaper than a dead crocodile.

lessons.title: Stress Reduction and Handling Techniques
lessons.body: Stress kills crocodiles. It lowers immunity, stops growth, and causes cannibalism. In Africa, heat and poor handling are the biggest stressors. Always approach a pen slowly. Never shout or run. Crocodiles sense vibrations. Use a noose pole to catch them, not your hands. For a small crocodile under 1 meter, use a net. For larger ones, two people with a noose and a shield. Cover the eyes with a damp cloth. This calms them. Keep handling time under 5 minutes. If you must move a crocodile, use a transport box with a lid. Line it with wet burlap. Do not put more than one crocodile per box unless they are from the same pen and similar size. During transport, keep temperature between 25Â°C and 30Â°C. If it is hotter, add ice packs wrapped in cloth. At the new site, release into a quiet pen with shade and clean water. Do not feed for 24 hours. Then offer a small fish. For daily care, feed at the same time each day. Crocodiles learn routines. Sudden changes cause stress. Keep noise low. Do not let dogs or children run around pens. Provide hiding places like pipes or logs. Stocking density should be one crocodile per 2 square meters for adults. Overcrowding causes fighting. Separate males during breeding. If you see a crocodile with its mouth open for long periods, it is too hot. Add shade or mist. If it stays in water all day, it may be too cold. Check temperature. Handle only when necessary. Every handling event should have a purpose: health check, move, or treatment. Never handle for fun. Train your workers in these techniques. A calm farm is a profitable farm.

lessons.title: Wound Care and Injury Management
lessons.body: Crocodiles fight. They get wounds from teeth, wire, and rough concrete. A small wound can become a fatal infection in days. When you see a wound, catch the crocodile safely. Wear gloves. Rinse the wound with clean water. Then clean with dilute povidone-iodine (1 part iodine to 10 parts water). Use a soft toothbrush to remove dirt. Do not use hydrogen peroxide; it damages tissue. For deep wounds, flush with saline solution. You can make saline: 1 teaspoon of salt in 1 liter of boiled water. After cleaning, apply a thick layer of honey. Honey kills bacteria and keeps the wound moist. Cover with a sterile gauze pad and tape it with medical tape. Change the dressing every 2 days. If the wound smells bad or has pus, start antibiotics: oxytetracycline 20 mg per kg injection every 3 days for 3 doses. For a broken jaw, you need a vet. Do not try to set it yourself. Keep the crocodile in a small, dry pen. Feed soft food like ground fish. For a missing limb, clean and bandage. It will heal but the crocodile may need to be separated permanently. For burns from heat lamps, apply silver sulfadiazine cream. Keep the animal out of water until healed. Check wounds daily. If you see maggots, remove them with tweezers and flush with iodine. Maggots mean the wound is old and dirty. In Africa, many wounds come from wire fencing. Replace wire with smooth electric fencing or concrete walls. Smooth all sharp edges. Keep pens clean. A wound that is treated early costs almost nothing. A wound left for three days can cost you the crocodile. Always have a first aid kit: iodine, honey, gauze, tape, antibiotics, and gloves.

lessons.title: Working with Veterinarians and Health Certificates
lessons.body: You cannot do everything alone. A good vet is your partner. In Africa, find a vet who works with wildlife or exotic animals. Call your local agriculture office or university. Ask for a vet who has crocodile experience. If none exists, find a vet willing to learn. You can share this module with them. Build a relationship before an emergency. Invite the vet to your farm once a year for a health check. Pay them fairly. A vet visit costs $100 to $300, but saves thousands. When you call, be ready with information: number of sick animals, symptoms, water temperature, and recent treatments. Have your records ready. The vet may need to take blood, swabs, or feces. Learn to restrain a crocodile for the vet. Use a noose pole and cover the eyes. The vet may prescribe drugs. Follow the dose exactly. Do not guess. If you need to transport a crocodile to a clinic, use a secure box with ventilation. Health certificates are required to sell or move crocodiles. In most African countries, you need a veterinary health certificate from a government vet. This certificate says the animals are free of disease. To get one, the vet inspects your farm and may test for specific diseases like salmonella. The certificate costs about $50 per batch. It is valid for 10 to 30 days. Keep copies. When you sell crocodiles, buyers will ask for this certificate. Without it, you cannot sell to zoos, restaurants, or export markets. Also, keep a farm health record book. Write down every vet visit, treatment, and death. This book proves you are a responsible farmer. It helps you get loans and grants. In Africa, many farmers fail because they do not keep records. Start today. A simple exercise book is enough.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Health Management and Veterinary Care for Crocodile Farming in Africa

Crocodile farming in Africaâwhether Nile crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus) production in South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Kenya, or Tanzaniaâis a business where animal health directly determines skin quality, meat yield, and export compliance. A single disease outbreak can wipe out months of feed investment and close export markets. This practical reference condenses the operational knowledge you need to keep your herd healthy, your mortality low, and your certificates valid.

The commercial reality is simple: crocodiles are hardy animals, but they are also stress-sensitive, temperature-dependent, and prone to bacterial infections when water quality or stocking density slips. Your profit margin lives or dies on prevention, not treatment. This module covers common diseases and parasites, preventive health programs, diagnosis and treatment, stress reduction and handling, wound care, and the paperwork that gets your skins and meat to market.

1. Common Diseases and Parasites

The most economically damaging conditions in African crocodile farms are bacterial infections (especially Aeromonas hydrophila, Salmonella spp., and Edwardsiella tarda), fungal infections (Saprolegnia), and parasitic infestations (coccidia, nematodes, and leeches). Stress-related diseasesâsuch as "crocodile pox" and systemic bacterial septicemiaâare often triggered by poor water quality, overcrowding, or temperature shock.

Nile crocodiles are particularly susceptible to Aeromonas septicemia when water temperatures drop below 25Â°C or when ammonia levels rise. In Zimbabwe and South Africa, Salmonella outbreaks have been linked to contaminated feed and have caused export rejections due to food safety concerns.

Table 1: Common Diseases and Parasites in African Crocodile Farms
Disease / Parasite Causative Agent Key Signs Economic Impact
SepticemiaAeromonas hydrophilaLethargy, red belly, sudden deathHigh mortality, skin rejection
SalmonellosisSalmonella spp.Diarrhea, dehydration, poor growthExport bans, food safety risk
Mycotic dermatitisSaprolegnia spp.White/grey patches on skinSkin downgrade
CoccidiosisEimeria spp.Weight loss, bloody fecesReduced growth rate
Leech infestationHirudineaVisible parasites, anemiaStress, secondary infection
NematodesAscaris spp.Poor condition, gut blockageMortality in juveniles

Source: Huchzermeyer, F.W. (2003). Crocodiles: Biology, Husbandry and Diseases. CABI Publishing; and FAO (2012). Farming of Nile Crocodile in Africa.

2. Preventive Health Programs and Vaccination

There are currently no commercially available vaccines for crocodiles in Africa. Prevention is therefore based on biosecurity, water quality management, nutrition, and stress reduction. A preventive health program should include:

  • Quarantine of new stock for 30â60 days.
  • Daily water quality monitoring (temperature, pH, ammonia, nitrite).
  • Regular disinfection of ponds and equipment.
  • Feed testing for Salmonella and mycotoxins.
  • Routine fecal sampling for parasites.
  • Vaccination is not standard, but autogenous bacterins have been used experimentally in South Africa.
â  SAFETY WARNING: Crocodiles are dangerous wild animals. Never handle them without trained personnel, proper restraints, and protective equipment. Any chemical treatment (e.g., formalin, potassium permanganate) must be used with correct dosage and personal protective equipment (PPE). Incorrect dosing can kill your entire stock and endanger workers. Always consult a registered veterinarian before administering any medication.

3. Diagnosing and Treating Infections

Diagnosis begins with daily observation. Look for changes in appetite, swimming behavior, skin color, and social interaction. A sick crocodile often isolates itself, floats listlessly, or refuses feed. Confirm diagnosis through laboratory testing: bacterial culture, sensitivity testing, fecal flotation, and blood smears.

Treatment must be prescribed by a veterinarian. Common antibiotics include oxytetracycline, enrofloxacin, and amoxicillin, but resistance is a growing problem. Never use human antibiotics without veterinary supervisionâthis is illegal in many African countries and contributes to antimicrobial resistance.

Table 2: Diagnostic and Treatment Reference for Common Crocodile Infections
Condition Diagnostic Method First-Line Treatment Withdrawal Period
Bacterial septicemiaBlood culture, sensitivityEnrofloxacin (vet prescribed)28 days
SalmonellosisFecal cultureOxytetracycline21 days
Fungal dermatitisSkin scraping, culturePotassium permanganate bathNone (topical)
CoccidiosisFecal flotationAmprolium14 days
Wounds/abscessesVisual, cultureDebridement + topical antibioticVaries

Source: South African Veterinary Council (2020). Guidelines for Antimicrobial Use in Food-Producing Animals; and Huchzermeyer (2003).

4. Stress Reduction and Handling Techniques

Stress is the silent killer in crocodile farming. It suppresses the immune system, reduces feed conversion, and causes skin damage. Key stress reduction practices include:

  • Maintain stable water temperature (28â32Â°C for optimal growth).
  • Avoid unnecessary handling; use restraint boards and blindfolds.
  • Handle during cool hours (early morning or evening).
  • Keep stocking density within recommended limits (e.g., 1 adult per 2â3 mÂ²).
  • Minimize noise and sudden movements around pens.
  • Use trained handlers only.

5. Wound Care and Injury Management

Wounds from fighting, biting, or rough handling are common. Immediate care prevents infection and skin downgrade. Steps:

  1. Isolate the injured animal.
  2. Clean wound with saline or dilute povidone-iodine.
  3. Debride dead tissue.
  4. Apply topical antibiotic (vet prescribed).
  5. Monitor for signs of systemic infection.
  6. Record all treatments for traceability.

6. Working with Veterinarians and Health Certificates

In most African countries, export of crocodile skins and meat requires a veterinary health certificate. This certificate confirms the animals were healthy, free from notifiable diseases, and slaughtered under hygienic conditions. Work with a registered veterinarian who understands crocodile medicine. Keep detailed records: feed logs, water quality logs, treatment records, mortality records, and visitor logs.

For export to the EU, you must comply with EU Regulation 2019/6 on veterinary medicinal products and EU Regulation 2017/625 on official controls. In South Africa, the Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development (DALRRD) issues health certificates. In Zimbabwe, the Department of Veterinary Services does the same.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Monitor water temperature, pH, ammonia, and nitrite daily.
  • Quarantine all new animals for at least 30 days.
  • Observe animals daily for signs of illness or injury.
  • Keep feed and water free from contamination.
  • Handle animals only when necessary, using trained staff and proper restraints.
  • Record all treatments, mortalities, and health events.
  • Work with a registered veterinarian for diagnosis and prescriptions.
  • Maintain valid health certificates for all exports.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Farming of Nile Crocodile in Africa (PDF)
  • South African Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development â Animal Health
  • World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) â Aquatic Animal Health Code
  • International Crocodile Farmers Association â Resources
  • FAO â Manual on the Production of Crocodile Skins

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills initiative. Always consult local veterinary authorities for country-specific regulations.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of bacterial infection in crocodiles?
quiz.explanation: Red belly is a classic sign of Aeromonas or Pseudomonas bacteria.

quiz.q: How long should you quarantine new crocodiles?
quiz.explanation: 30 days quarantine helps prevent introducing diseases to your farm.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dose of praziquantel for internal parasites?
quiz.explanation: Praziquantel at 5 mg per kg of body weight is effective against tapeworms.

quiz.q: Which water parameter must stay below 0.5 mg per liter?
quiz.explanation: High ammonia burns gills and causes stress; keep it below 0.5 mg/L.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to calm a crocodile during handling?
options: B) Cover its eyes with a damp cloth
D) Put it in direct sun
quiz.explanation: Covering the eyes reduces stress and makes handling safer.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm crocodiles in a preventive program?
quiz.explanation: Deworming every 3 months with fenbendazole controls internal parasites.

quiz.q: What is the first step when you find a wounded crocodile?
options: B) Catch it safely and rinse the wound
quiz.explanation: Safe capture and cleaning prevent infection from worsening.

quiz.q: Which natural product is recommended for wound care?
quiz.explanation: Honey has antibacterial properties and keeps wounds moist.

quiz.q: What is the maximum stocking density for adult crocodiles?
quiz.explanation: One adult per 2 square meters reduces fighting and stress.

quiz.q: What should you do if a crocodile has maggots in a wound?
options: B) Remove with tweezers and flush with iodine
quiz.explanation: Maggots indicate a dirty wound; remove them and disinfect.

quiz.q: Which antibiotic is commonly used for infections in crocodiles?
quiz.explanation: Oxytetracycline at 20 mg/kg is a broad-spectrum antibiotic for reptiles.

quiz.q: How often should you change wound dressings?
quiz.explanation: Changing dressings every 2 days keeps the wound clean and allows healing.

quiz.q: What is a sign of heat stress in a crocodile?
options: A) Mouth open for long periods
quiz.explanation: Open mouth is a cooling behavior; if prolonged, add shade or mist.

quiz.q: Why is a veterinary health certificate important?
options: A) It is required to sell or move crocodiles
B) It makes crocodiles grow faster
D) It is only for decoration
quiz.explanation: Health certificates prove disease-free status and are needed for sales and transport.

quiz.q: What should you do before a vet visit?
options: B) Prepare records and restrain a crocodile
C) Clean the whole farm with bleach
quiz.explanation: Having records and a restrained animal helps the vet work efficiently.

quiz.q: How can you make saline solution for wound flushing?
options: A) 1 teaspoon salt in 1 liter boiled water
B) 1 cup salt in 1 liter water
C) 1 tablespoon sugar in 1 liter water
quiz.explanation: This approximate isotonic solution is safe for flushing wounds.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of wounds in crocodile pens?
quiz.explanation: Wire fencing can cut skin; use smooth walls or electric fencing.

quiz.q: What is the recommended treatment for fungal infections?
quiz.explanation: A 2 mg/L potassium permanganate dip for 10 minutes treats fungus.

quiz.q: How long should you keep a crocodile out of water after wound treatment?
quiz.explanation: Water can introduce bacteria; keep the animal dry until the wound closes.

quiz.q: What is a sign of internal parasites?
quiz.explanation: Tapeworm segments appear in feces; treat with praziquantel.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid handling crocodiles for fun?
options: A) It causes stress and can lead to disease
B) It makes them grow faster
quiz.explanation: Unnecessary handling stresses crocodiles and lowers immunity.

quiz.q: What is the maximum handling time for a crocodile?
quiz.explanation: Keep handling under 5 minutes to reduce stress.

quiz.q: What should you do if a crocodile is not eating for one day?
quiz.explanation: One day without food is an early warning; isolate and watch for other signs.

quiz.q: Which vitamin or mineral is important for wound healing?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin C supports collagen formation and immune function.

quiz.q: How often should you test water for ammonia?
quiz.explanation: Weekly testing catches dangerous ammonia spikes early.

quiz.q: What is a good biosecurity measure?
options: C) Allowing visitors to touch crocodiles
D) Feeding raw meat from unknown sources
quiz.explanation: Footbaths reduce pathogen spread between pens.

quiz.q: What should you do with a dead crocodile?
options: A) Record symptoms and dispose safely
C) Feed it to other crocodiles
D) Leave it in the pen
quiz.explanation: Recording data helps diagnose herd health; dispose to prevent disease spread.

quiz.q: What is the dose of oxytetracycline for crocodiles?
quiz.explanation: 20 mg per kg body weight is a standard antibiotic dose for reptiles.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important in crocodile health?
options: A) It helps identify disease patterns and get loans
B) It is required by law
C) It makes crocodiles grow faster
quiz.explanation: Records show treatment outcomes and support farm management decisions.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a healthy crocodile?
options: A) Clear eyes and pink gums
quiz.explanation: Clear eyes and pink gums indicate good health.
